stops.name: Assisi, Piazza del Comune, the neighbors' question
stops.campa: Her son is king of the revels now, baton in hand, leading the youth of Assisi through the night streets singing troubadour songs in French, her songs; the town cannot tell where the mother's voice ends and the son's begins. The neighbors marvel and needle her: what will this spendthrift of yours come to? She answers them like one prompted by a divine oracle, serene above the noise of the tripudianti. She has seen the end of the performance the rest of the piazza takes for waste. The fire she carried over the Alps is alight and singing.
stops.quote: How think you that this son of mine will turn out? Be assured that he will become a son of God by his merits.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 3 (trans. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908)

stops.name: Assisi, the news from Collestrada
stops.campa: War with Perugia, and the commune's cavalry rides out with the merchant's son in bright armor among them. Then the news climbs the hill: the men of Assisi broken at Collestrada, the fields red down to Ponte San Giovanni, the dead unransomed and the ransomable roped off toward Perugia. Her son is alive because his armor priced him. Pica knows the doctrine for this hour: the fourth suffering, when love lacks the power to seize its blessing, and its remedy, almsgiving; and the house opens its purse toward Perugia. The long waiting begins.

stops.name: Perugia, the ransom
stops.campa: A year the boy lies in the pits of Perugia, and the mother treats for him across the war. In the dungeon, the returning prisoners say, he laughs and sings in his chains until his fellow captives think him mad, and prophesies that one day the whole world will adore him. The fever of the pits is in him when Pietro's ransom at last unlocks the irons: tubercular, wasted, twenty-two. Pica receives back a son whose body has been broken open into strangeness. She paid the merchant's price for him; what comes home no ledger can price.

stops.name: Assisi, the sickbed
stops.campa: Through the long convalescence she nurses him, broth, poultices, and the old pharmacy of the finca: songs. When he can walk he goes out on a stick to look at the countryside he loved, and comes home appalled: the vines, Subasio, the plain toward Foligno have gone flat and stale and give him nothing. Pica hears him say it and does not despair, for she knows the symptom from Pierre's catechism: this is the fifth suffering beginning, the open heart, the wound of a love about to be returned. Its remedy is prayer, and he begins to pray.

stops.name: San Damiano, bread by a hidden hand
stops.campa: Her son has heard the painted crucifix of San Damiano speak his name and command him: go, repair my house, which is falling wholly into ruin; and hides now from his father's rage in a secret cave, then among the ruins, a hermit at the margin of the town, keeping company with lepers. Someone of the household (the legend leaves the hand unnamed, and devotion has always folded it into Pica) carries him bread in secret. The command from the cross is her own vision returned: the fire that repairs the crumbling church. She feeds it quietly.

stops.name: Assisi, the cellar, the chains, and the freeing
stops.campa: Pietro drags his son home by force, beats him, binds him, and locks him chained in the dark of the cellar, sure that misery will cure vocation. Then business calls the merchant abroad. His wife, left alone at home with the prisoner, speaks gently to him and sees she cannot move him from his purpose; and she yearns over him with maternal compassion, and she looses his chains and lets him go free. Pietro returns, rages, and turns on her, heaping sin upon sin. Assisi will remember which parent held which tool: the bronze at the Chiesa Nuova puts the cloth in his hands, and the chain in hers.

stops.name: Assisi, the renunciation before the bishop
stops.campa: Pietro hauls his son before Bishop Guido in the court by Santa Maria Maggiore to disinherit him and recover his money, and the mother stands in the crowd of all Assisi. She watches the boy return the coins, and then everything: he strips naked before the city, lays even his clothes at his father's feet, and from under the bishop's mantle declares the exchange of fathers. What Pica hears is exact: he has renounced Bernardone: the name, the cloth, the shop, the status. He has not renounced, and cannot renounce, the blood that came over the Alps singing.

stops.name: Assisi, the consolation of Giovanna
stops.campa: She finds her son poor, shorn and radiant, and gives him the speech the corpus keeps whole: they have the same name; the inner fire of poets, bards and troubadours is an inheritance no bishop's court can strip. She tells him his road: beneath the cross to the land of the prophets; weakness his strength and his greatness; the sweet flame of his suffering spreading until the world speaks of him only as Francesco; the fire tempering fractured hearts, repairing the crumbling church, restoring the faith. Every clause will come true, and the canon will count the fulfillments one by one.
stops.quote: Tenemos el mismo nombre. Yo soy Giovanna y tú eres Giovanni. Somos John, Joan, Jeanne y Juana. Tenemos el mismo corazón, como la Virgen y el Lord. Compartimos un fuego interior de poetas, bardos y trovadores. Siempre eres mi hijo y un Bourlémont. Viajarás bajo la cruz a la tierra de los profetas. La debilidad será tu fuerza y tu grandeza. La dulce llama de tu sufrimiento se extenderá cuando la gente hable de ti solo por el nombre de Francisco. Este fuego templará los corazones fracturados, reparará la iglesia que se desmorona y restaurará la fe.

stops.name: San Damiano, the mother at the walls
stops.campa: He turns mason below the town, begging stones like a jongleur crying wares, and the lady of the cloth-house comes down the olive path to watch her son at his masonry. He works singing, in French, always in French when the joy is on him, and prophesies aloud that ladies will one day live here whose fame will glorify the whole Church. She hears her own tongue carrying his first architecture. The gaya ciencia she brought from Provence has become load-bearing: song setting stone. It is the last picture of the two of them that any tradition affords.

stops.name: Assisi, the first ending: dead by 1211
stops.campa: Here the record forks, and both roads are kept. In the Assisi ledgers she simply ceases: by 1211 her son Angelo, Angelo di Pica in every act, never Angelo di Pietro, names his own son Picone, remaking his mother in a name, as the custom marks the dead. If the parchment is right, she never saw the Rule approved in Rome, never heard of Greccio or La Verna; she died while her son was still the town's scandal, and the prophecy still a mother's word against the evidence. The acts do not say where she lies. No stone, no parish book, no shrine has ever claimed her body.

stops.name: Assisi, the second ending: the widow of the cord
stops.campa: The other canon gives her years and a habit: she outlives Pietro and, widowed, dons the penitential garb of her son's Third Order, living secluded in piety and prayer, the first mother inside the brotherhood she made possible. Around her waist goes the cord whose hanging knot holds five loops: the five sufferings Pierre sang at the finca, become the five wounds her son will carry home from La Verna, the knot the friars will one day carry to Cusco to meet the quipu. Franciscan custom keeps her as Blessed Pica, on the fourteenth of April, by love and not by decree.

stops.name: Assisi, no tomb: the open silence
stops.campa: On the night her son dies singing at the Porziuncola, larks wheeling over the hut at dusk, no chronicle sets his mother anywhere: at the bedside, in the crowd, or in a grave. That is the whole of it: no burial tradition exists for Pica in any church, register or legend; the town that keeps his sandals and her chain keeps no stone for her. The journey ends in that open silence, unclosed, like a knot left untied at the end of a cord. Only the name goes on, downriver of the castle where it began: Giovanna, Giovanni, John; and waiting at the Fairy Tree, Jeanne, and beyond her, Juana.
